This paper presents the first dataset with RGB+Depth+Thermal modalities, for the task of object tracking. The dataset contains 500 videos and around 200K tri-modal frames, with ground truth bounding boxes. Additionally, the authors trained a model in their dataset leveraging the three modalities, and outperform all existing bi- and uni-modal baselines, setting the state of the art and nicely motivating the benefit of multimodality. 

The authors addressed satisfactorily the issues found by the reviewers in their original reviews. Among others, the authors clarified the ethical concerns regarding privacy and humans, provided requested results with additional baselines (HMFT, Untrack, DCEvo, OSTrack, SeqTrack, MixViT and MCITrack), cross-dataset results (in RGBD1K) and runtime analysis, provided additional details and analysis on their proposed architecture, and clarified technical details regarding the different modality resolutions or stereo results in low lighting. The discussion and the new material contributed to further motivate and validate the contributions of the paper, both the data and the model.

We sincerely thank all reviewers and ethics reviewers for their constructive, insightful, and encouraging feedback throughout the review process. We greatly appreciate the recognition of value of the RGBDT500 dataset, the novelty and effectiveness of the RDTTrack framework, and our efforts toward reproducibility, clarity, and responsible research practices.

Regarding the ethics reviews, we have fully addressed concerns on consent, privacy, and potential dual-use risks, by clarifying our data collection protocols, confirming informed consent for all identifiable individuals, ensuring anonymization when needed, and committing to a research-only, non-commercial license with explicit safeguards. Ethics Reviewer yQcH confirmed that our revisions and promised additions in the final paper adequately addressed the concerns, and Ethics Reviewer RA9h noted that all issues can be addressed with minor textual additions.

On the technical side, we thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions on expanding baselines, deepening theoretical analysis, performing cross-dataset validation, and adding efficiency and failure case analyses. We have incorporated additional experiments, including comparisons with Un-Track, image-level fusion tracking method, and recent SOTA RGB trackers, enhanced theoretical discussions, extended evaluations to public RGB-D benchmark, and provided detailed runtime and failure case analyses. Reviewers confirmed that these updates addressed their concerns, with one noting an improvement in rating and one noting that the rating remained positive.

We are encouraged by the reviewers’ overall satisfaction with our responses and will implement all promised revisions to ensure the final manuscript meets the highest standards of technical rigor, transparency, and ethical responsibility. Once again, we thank the reviewers for their time, expertise, and constructive engagement, which have greatly strengthened our work.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the detailed concerns. We take these ethical responsibilities seriously and acknowledge that our prior manuscript lacked sufficient transparency. Below, we provide detailed clarifications and corrections addressing each point raised.

**Q1: Correction of Q10 Broader Impacts**\
**A1:** This work enhances the robustness of multi-modal tracking, presenting both potential positive and negative societal impacts. On the positive side, it can enable life-saving applications such as improving autonomous vehicle safety in adverse weather conditions and advancing wildlife monitoring efforts. Conversely, the enhanced tracking capabilities across RGB, depth, and thermal domains may be misused in surveillance systems, including mass monitoring, protest tracking, or law enforcement applications that could infringe on privacy and civil liberties. Due to the dual-use nature of this technology, it requires responsible development frameworks and ethical deployment guidelines to mitigate risks such as privacy violations.  We will revise the answers in the checklist and update the paper to include a discussion of the potential positive and negative societal impacts.

**Q2: Correction of Q11 Safeguards**\
**A2:** We will revise our response to checklist Q11 to accurately reflect that the proposed technology does pose potential risks related to surveillance applications. We explicitly acknowledge the dual-use nature of our tracking system, particularly its capability to function under low-light and occluded conditions, which could be misused for pervasive surveillance by state or non-state actors. We are committed to mitigating such risks through a research-only, non-commercial license, access restrictions, and clear usage guidelines.

**Q3: Consent and anonymization techniques**\
**A3:** We confirm that informed consent was obtained for all individuals appearing in the RGBDT500 dataset. The dataset was collected in controlled environments, primarily featuring non-identifiable household objects and animals. In the rare instances where individuals appear, they are members of our research and data collection team, who are fully informed and give explicit consent to be included. No bystanders or members of the public are recorded without consent. Furthermore, any content containing potentially identifying information are manually reviewed and either excluded or anonymized through face or feature blurring. We will include this clarification in the paper’s data collection section and ethics statement.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and responsible feedback on the ethical aspects of our work. We take these concerns seriously, and will carefully address each point to ensure clarity, transparency, and alignment with the NeurIPS ethics guidelines in the final version of the paper. Below is our detailed response.

**Q1: Consent & IRB**\
**A1:** The RGBDT500 dataset was collected in controlled environments, with a focus on non-identifiable household objects and animals. In rare scenarios where individuals appear in the dataset, those individuals were members of our research and data collection team, who were fully aware of the recording and gave explicit consent to be included. No bystanders or members of the public were captured without consent. Furthermore, all frames were reviewed to ensure that no identifiable facial features or license plates are present in the released dataset. Any content with even potential identifiers is either excluded or manually anonymized through blurring. We will include this clarification in the paper’s data collection section and ethics statement.

**Q2: Privacy notice**\
**A2:** All sequences involving public capture occurred in areas where photography is legally permitted. For any such sequences, signage was displayed to indicate that recording was taking place for academic research purposes. Additionally, we will set up a dedicated contact email where individuals can request takedown of specific sequences if they believe they are represented. We will make these practices documented in the final version of the paper.

**Q3: Responsible release**\
**A3:** The RGBDT500 dataset will be released under a research-only, non-commercial license. This license explicitly prohibits any use for continuous surveillance, military targeting, or deployment in real-time monitoring systems. To enforce responsible use, when the data is officially released, access to the dataset will require users to accept the terms via a click-through agreement, which includes clauses that:
- Limit use strictly to academic, non-commercial research purposes,
- Forbid redistribution or integration into downstream surveillance tools,
- Prohibit use in applications involving privacy infringement, crowd tracking, or law enforcement targeting,
- Require proper citation and attribution in any derivative work.
These statements will be included in the paper and the license terms.

**Q4: Dataset card**\
**A4:** We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to include a structured dataset card and agree that transparency regarding the dataset’s composition is critical.
- Geographic distribution: Data was collected across distinct regions, including urban, suburban, and indoor lab settings, representing diverse environments and sensor conditions.
- Day/Night ratio: Approximately 80% of the sequences were recorded during the day and 20% at night, to reflect a variety of lighting scenarios.
- Demographic information: As the dataset primarily includes objects and animals in controlled environments, demographic attributes are not labeled or applicable. In rare cases involving people, subjects were team members who provided consent, and no demographic classification was performed.
- Fairness audit plan: While demographic analysis is not applicable for this version of the dataset, we include a short plan to expand fairness auditing in future iterations. This includes evaluating the dataset’s impact in downstream models, e.g., bias in object tracking under varying conditions, and inviting feedback from users to inform gaps in representativeness.

**Q5: Negative societal impacts and mitigations.**\
**A5:** While our work focuses on tracking non-identifiable objects, we acknowledge the potential for misuse in surveillance contexts. For example, it might be misused for mass monitoring, protest tracking, or law enforcement applications that could infringe on privacy and civil liberties. To mitigate such risks, the RGBDT500 dataset will be released under a research-only, non-commercial license that explicitly prohibits use for surveillance, military, or law enforcement purposes. Access will require click-through acceptance of these terms. All sequences involving individuals feature team members with explicit consent, and no identifiable information is present. We encourage transparency and welcome community feedback to support responsible use. We will add a Societal and Ethical Impacts section to the paper, which discusses possible negative impacts and clearly discourages any use that may infringe on privacy or civil rights.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for recognizing the value of our tri-modal dataset RGBDT500 and the adaptability of the RDTTrack tracker. 
We also appreciate the positive feedback on our ablation studies.

**Q1: Comparison with VTUAV dataset.**\
**A1:** 
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. 
In the paper, we have already provided a comparison with 11 popular tracking datasets in Table 1.
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we have additionally included a comparison with VTUAV datatset, as shown in the table below.
|Dataset|RGB | Depth|TIR|Sequences|Frames|Classes|Training Set|
|  -----|------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|------|
| VTUAV| ✓ |✗|✓ |500 |1.7M | 13 |✓|
| RGBDT500| ✓ | ✓| ✓ |500 |203.7K | 66 |✓ |

As shown, RGBDT500 augments the data modalities  by including depth, and features more diverse object classes, while maintaining the same number of sequences. 
Despite having fewer frames, RGBDT500 is designed to cover a wider variety of scenes and modality interactions, making it complementary to VTUAV, which focuses on UAV-based RGB-T scenarios.
We will include this comparison and discussion in the final version.

**Q2: Evaluation of HMFT.**\
**A2:** 
We have evaluated the HMFT tracker on RGBDT500. The results are presented below.
|Tracker|AUC | DP|
|-------|--------|-------|
| HMFT|0.469 |0.388 |

As shown, HMFT achieves an AUC of 0.469 and a DP of 0.388 on RGBDT500, likely due to its design being optimized  for UAV-based RGB-T tracking scenarios, whereas RGBDT500 features more diverse ground-level scenes.
These results will be included in the final version to provide a more comprehensive comparison across tracking methods.

**Q3: Dataset code accessibility**\
**A3:** 
We would like to clarify that both the dataset and code have been made accessible. 
To improve accessibility, we have updated the GitHub repository with detailed usage instructions, and have also added a link to a newly created dataset website.
We will make sure that these resources are more clearly referenced and easy to access in the final version of the paper.

Below, we address each of the reviewer’s concerns in detail.

**Q1: Lack of comparison with image-level fusion tracking methods.**\
**A1:** Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have incorporated a representative RGB-T image-level fusion method, DCEvo [1], with a unimodal tracker OSTrack to form an image-level fusion tracking pipeline. 
The results are presented below.
|Tracker|AUC | DP|
|----------|--------|-------|
| OSTrack| 0.694 |   0.736 |
| DCEvo+OSTrack| 0.706 |   0.741 |

As shown, the image-level fusion of RGB and thermal infrared inputs significantly enhances the performance of the unimodal tracker OSTrack.
We will include a more detailed discussion and comparisons with image-level fusion tracking methods in the final version of the paper.

[1] Discriminative Cross-Dimensional Evolutionary Learning for Infrared and Visible Image Fusion. CVPR, 2025.

**Q2: Failure case analysis and error attribution.**\
**A2:** We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. 
We agree that analyzing failure cases is essential for understanding the limitations of our model, and consequently have conducted a preliminary examination of representative failure samples.
Our observations indicate that RDTTrack is particularly vulnerable to the target re-appearance after long-term heavy occlusions.
We believe that introducing temporal modeling mechanisms, such as temporal attention or memory modules, could help mitigate this issue by leveraging motion continuity and history cues.
We will include a detailed failure case analysis and discuss potential future improvements in the final version of the paper.

**Q3: Lack of runtime and efficiency analysis.**\
**A3:** For efficiency comparison, we have conducted runtime evaluations of several trackers using Frames Per Second (FPS) as the metric. All experiments are run on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, and the results are presented below.
|Tracker|RDTTrack | BAT|TBSI|SDSTrack|Un-Track|ViPT|
|  -----|------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| FPS| 76.6 | 26.8 |32.5 |20.9 |41.2 |31.8 |

As shown, RDTTrack achieves significantly higher runtime efficiency compared to other recent multi-modal trackers, reaching 76.6 FPS.
This achievement is owes to the use of lightweight prompt learning and a frozen baseline, which reduces the number of additional parameters and the resulting computational overhead.
In addition, the RDTTrack model contains only 0.86 million trainable parameters, making it highly efficient for training as well.
We will include this efficiency analysis and discussion in the final version of the paper.

**Q4: Possible solutions for work limitations.**\
**A4:** We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. 
The current version of the RGBDT500 dataset is designed specifically for multi-modal single-object tracking, and each sequence includes annotations for only one target.
However, real-world scenarios often involve multiple objects and more complex tasks.
In  future work, RGBDT500 can be extended through additional annotations to provide support for a broader range of tasks, such as multi-modal object detection, multi-object tracking, fine-grained object localization, and cross-modal super-resolution.
These potential directions will be explicitly discussed in the final version of the paper.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for recognizing the contributions of our tri-modal dataset and the design of the multi-modal fusion and prompt learning modules. 
We are glad that the effectiveness and potential impact of our approach on future multi-modal tracking research are well appreciated.
Below, we respond to the concerns in detail.

**Q1: Resolution discrepancy across modalities and its effect on performance.**\
**A1:** We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding resolution differences. 
As described in Section 3.1 of the paper, RGB and depth images are captured using a ZED stereo camera, while thermal infrared (TIR) images are acquired separately with an LGCS121 thermal camera. 
The raw RGB, depth, and TIR streams are temporally synchronized, but only the RGB-depth pairs are natively pixel-aligned.
The RGB and depth images have a resolution of 1920×1080, while the original TIR images are captured at 640×512, resulting in inherent resolution and field-of-view mismatches.
To ensure spatial alignment, we apply a manual feature point based matrix mapping to achieve spatial registration and re-scale the TIR images. 
This registration strategy is consistent with practices adopted in recent benchmark datasets, such as the VTUAV dataset [1].
In addition, due to the field-of-view mismatch, we adopt a zero-filling strategy for TIR images in areas not covered by its field of view. 
This design choice preserves the full spatial extent of the RGB/depth views, which typically offer wider coverage and richer contextual information, thereby benefiting the tracker’s performance in complex scenes.

To assess the impact of down sampling and zero-padding strategies, we conducted an experiment using different input resolutions of the RGBDT500 dataset to train and evaluate RDTTrack. The results are presented below.
|Resolution|AUC | DP|
|-------|--------|-------|
| 1920×1080|   0.752 |   0.792 |
| 640×512 	 |  0.745 |  0.790|

As shown, the performance differences are marginal. 
Nevertheless, we opt to preserve the higher-resolution format, 1920×1080, in the final benchmark, as it enables more diverse future research directions, such as fine-grained object localization, multi-modal segmentation, and cross-modal super-resolution.

[1] Visible-Thermal UAV Tracking: A Large-Scale Benchmark and New Baseline. CVPR, 2022.

**Q2: Use of dated RGB-only baselines and missing OSTrack in Table 2.**\
**A2:** Thank you for pointing this out. While Table 2 includes a range of established RGB-only trackers, we agree that the omission of baseline OSTrack and current RGB SOTA trackers may lead to an incomplete comparison.
To rectify, the results for OSTrack on RGBDT500 are included in Table 3, where the tracker achieves an AUC of 0.694 and DP of 0.736.
We will revise the manuscript by including the OSTrack performance in Table 2.

Regarding more recent RGB-only methods, we have followed the reviewer's suggestion and conducted  an additional  comparison with SeqTrack [2], MixViT [3] and MCITrack [4]. The results are shown below.
|Tracker|Publication|AUC | DP|
|----------|--------|--------|-------|
| OSTrack|ECCV2022| 0.694 |   0.736 |
| SeqTrack 	|CVPR2023|  0.719 |  0.766|
| MixFormer	 |IEEE-TPAMI2024 |0.732 |  0.781|
| MCITrack|AAAI2025 |  0.741 |  0.788|

As shown, the current SOTA RGB-only trackers outperform our baseline model, OSTrack. However, our proposed RDTTrack consistently achieves higher AUC and DP scores than these strong RGB-only methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of our tri-modal fusion strategy.
We will include these new results and the corresponding analysis in the final version of the paper.

[2] Seqtrack: Sequence to Sequence Learning for Visual Object Tracking. CVPR, 2023.\
[3] MixFormer: End-to-End Tracking with Iterative Mixed Attention. IEEE TPAMI, 2024.\
[4] Exploring Enhanced Contextual Information for Video-Level Object Tracking. AAAI, 2025.

**Q3: Use of stereo-based depth and its limitations under low-light conditions.**\
**A3:** We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding the ZED stereo camera’s reduced accuracy in low-light scenarios. 
Indeed, stereo-based depth estimation relies heavily on texture and illumination, which may degrade under such conditions.
The thermal modality is specifically designed to compensate for such degradation, which is one of the motivations for tri-modal fusion. 
In our dataset, we intentionally include challenging low-light sequences to highlight this interaction.
In addition, as illustrated in Fig.1, stereo-based depth remains reasonably effective for close-range objects, even in dim lighting, due to sufficient residual texture and disparity.
Using structured-light sensors, e.g., Intel RealSense, is an excellent suggestion. 
In future work, we will compare stereo-derived depth with structured-light-based depth in selected low-light sequences, to quantify the role of depth fidelity in enhancing the contribution of the thermal modality.

**Q4: Dataset documentation, code instructions, and dataset website.**\
**A4:** We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions regarding dataset documentation and code instructions.
In response, we have updated the GitHub repository to include detailed usage instructions, including guidance on dataset structure, loading scripts, and usage. 
Additionally, we have created a dedicated dataset website that provides an overview, download links, and documentation for RGBDT500. 
The entry point to this website is clearly linked from the updated GitHub repository that was originally submitted with the paper.
We hope these updates improve the usability and clarity of our dataset for the community, and we appreciate the reviewer’s feedback that prompted these improvements.

We greatly appreciate the reviewer's recognition of our novel tri-modal tracking approach and of the value of the RGBDT500 dataset enabling multi-modal tracking research.
Thank you also for acknowledging our efforts to promote reproducibility and open-sourcing all resources to facilitate community verification and extension. Below, we respond to the concerns in detail.

**Q1: Experimental comparison with Un-Track.**\
**A1:** In this work, in addition to comparing with ViPT,  we have also evaluated the proposed RDTTrack against several state-of-the-art multi-modal trackers, including SPT, TBSI, BAT, SDSTrack, etc.
The experimental results and discussions demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of RDTTrack.
In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have also conducted a comparative experiment with Un-Track on RGBDT500, as shown in the table.

|Tracker |AUC | DP|
|-------|--------|-------|
| Untrack-RGBT   |  0.732 | 0.790 |
| Untrack-RGBD  |  0.733 | 0.776 |
| RDTTrack	 | 0.752  | 0.792 |

The results show that UnTrack-RGBT achieves an AUC of 0.732 and a DP of 0.790, while UnTrack-RGBD achieves a slightly higher AUC of 0.733 but a lower DP of 0.776.
The updated results demonstrate that our RDTTrack outperforms Un-Track, achieving higher AUC and DP scores, highlighting the potential benefit of tri-modal fusion.
These results and corresponding discussions of Un-Track will be included in the final version.

**Q2: Deeper theoretical analysis of the fusion approach.**\
**A2:** 
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment.
To address the reviewer's concern regarding the theoretical analysis of our fusion approach, we will enhance the manuscript with a detailed explanation of both the orthogonal constraint and prompt learning module, supported by foundational literature in multi-modal representation learning.

For the orthogonal constraints applied to depth-thermal feature fusion, our method enforces orthogonality between modality-specific features to reduce redundancy and enhance the complementary information.
Specifically, depth features capture the geometric structure of objects, while thermal features reflect radiative heat patterns.
These modalities are inherently distinct, and forcing orthogonality encourages the model to learn non-overlapping, modality-specific sub-spaces.
This design is theoretically grounded in sub-space alignment principles, where orthogonal projection ensures that depth and thermal features span disjoint sub-spaces.
As a result, the information overlap is minimized, and feature discriminability enhanced.
Our approach is inspired by the orthogonal loss formulation in [1], where orthogonality has been shown to eliminate redundant information across modalities and improve the multi-modal fusion performance.

For prompt learning, our module leverages the pre-trained OSTrack model as a frozen knowledge repository, where fused RGB-depth-thermal features act as dynamic prompts to adapt the model to tri-modal inputs without inducing catastrophic forgetting.
This aligns with the pre-train, prompt and predict paradigm, wherein lightweight prompts condition a frozen model to retrieve task-relevant representations.
The generalization capability arises from the stability of the pre-trained baseline representations and the lightweight adaptability of the prompt module.
As highlighted  in the foundational prompt survey in [2] and other works [3], such design enables efficient knowledge transfer across tasks and modalities while preserving robustness.
We will revise the paper to include these theoretical insights, and add references to related frameworks in the final version.

[1] Orthogonalization-Guided Feature Fusion Network for Multimodal 2D+3D Facial Expression Recognition. IEEE TMM, 2021.\
[2] Pre-train, Prompt, and Predict: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Methods in Natural Language Processing. ACM Computing Surveys, 2023.\
[3] Visual Prompt Tuning. ECCV, 2022.


**Q3: Cross-dataset experiments.**\
**A3:** We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. 
Our  primary  focus in this work was to validate tri-modal fusion for tracking under new conditions not covered by existing two-modal benchmarks, which led us to prioritize RGBDT500.
However, we agree that cross-dataset evaluation is crucial for verifying robustness.
To this end, we have evaluated RDTTrack on the public RGB-D tracking benchmark RGBD1K using the official Precision, Recall and F-score as evaluation metrics. The results are shown below.
|Tracker |Precision | Recall| F-Score|
|-------|--------|-------|-------|
| OSTrack |   0.489 |   0.516 | 0.502 |
| ViPT|  0.453 |  0.472| 0.462 |
| RDTTrack | 0.501  | 0.531| 0.516|

As shown, RDTTrack outperforms both, baseline OSTrack and ViPT-RGBD, on RGBD1K.
The comparison demonstrates RDTTrack’s generalization capability in multi-modal tracking.
We will extend the evaluation to additional RGB-D and RGB-T benchmarks and include the results and analysis in the final version of the paper.

**Q4: Ethical concerns.**\
**A4:**  We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and responsible feedback regarding ethical considerations.
We take ethical considerations seriously.
The RGBDT500 dataset is captured in controlled environments, primarily featuring mostly non-identifiable household objects and animals.
For the limited sequences that involve individuals,  we have obtained explicit consent from those participants.
The dataset contains no sensitive or personally identifiable information, and is intended solely for academic research purposes.
All equipment used, including the ZED stereo camera and thermal infrared camera, was operated under standard safety and privacy protocols to ensure ethical and responsible data collection and handling.
A detailed ethical impact statement will be included in the final version of the paper.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.  I am unclear why the authors compare only with ViPT and do not include Untrack [1], which is more directly focused on universal RGB-X fusion. Unless there is a compelling reason, Untrack should be included as a baseline in the experimental comparison.

2. The paper lacks deeper theoretical or mechanistic analysis of its fusion approach (e.g., orthogonal constraints, prompt learning modules). The effectiveness is mainly supported by experiments, without detailed explanation of generalization or robustness principles.

3. The evaluation is mostly limited to the new dataset. There is a lack of cross-dataset experiments on existing public RGB-D or RGB-T benchmarks. In addition, there are no detailed experiments analyzing the fusion mechanisms (such as orthogonal constraints or prompt learning) on other public datasets, which would better demonstrate the generalizability and robustness of the proposed approach.

summary.value: This paper introduces a trimodal benchmark dataset for single-object tracking under low-light conditions, integrating RGB, depth (D), and thermal (TIR) data. The authors contribute not only a well-synchronized dataset, but also a depth–thermal fusion module and a prompt learning framework to adapt existing trackers to the new modality combination while keeping the number of trainable parameters low. Their method achieves state-of-the-art performance across several benchmarks, demonstrating the benefit of combining modalities in low-light scenarios. The strengths of this work lie in its data diversity and cross-modality alignment, which form a strong basis for advancing multimodal tracking.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.	In the single-object tracking domain, the authors temporally align data from three modalities—RGB, depth, and thermal—laying a solid foundation for future multimodal fusion research.
2.	Alongside introducing a new dataset, they design a depth-TIR fusion module for existing trackers and employ prompt learning to reduce trainable parameters. This adaptation fits the new dataset well and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.	The three modalities differ in resolution. For example, the TIR image in Figure 1 is clearly lower-resolution than the RGB-D image. During training, are RGB-D frames down-sampled to match TIR resolution, or is the TIR image zero-padded? How do these choices affect performance?
2.	The RGB-only baselines in Table 2 are dated (2019–2022). Results from current RGB SOTA trackers are missing. Moreover, the prompt-learning design uses OSTrack as its baseline, yet OSTrack itself is absent from the table, so it is unclear whether RGB + D + T fusion truly surpasses a strong RGB-only baseline.
3.	Table 3 shows that RGB + D + T achieves the best results with RDTTracker. However, the depth data were captured with a ZED stereo camera, whose depth estimates are nearly invalid under low-light conditions. Depth cameras based on structured light (e.g., Intel RealSense) are immune to low-light issues. Would using ground-truth depth from a structured-light sensor—independent of ambient illumination—give the thermal modality an even greater advantage under the low-light scenarios highlighted in the paper?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: There are no significant ethical concerns identified in this work. The data collection process appears to follow standard protocols, and no sensitive or personally identifiable information is involved. The research focuses on technical advancements without introducing potential risks to individuals or society.

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is accessible via a Google Drive link, but it lacks descriptive documentation, and the GitHub repository does not provide usage instructions.

additional_feedback.value: It would be better to have a dedicated dataset website along with documentation that explains how to use the dataset.

final_justification.value:
The clarification on how RGB-D and TIR resolutions are handled during training resolves my concern about mismatched inputs.
The additional results you provided for current SOTA RGB trackers, which also underpin your prompt-learning design, address my request for SOTA RGB-only baselines.
I agree that a controlled comparison between stereo depth (ZED) and structured-light depth (e.g., RealSense) is outside the current scope given hardware differences and data re-collection needs. Your plan to validate this in follow-up experiments is reasonable; a brief note in the paper acknowledging this limitation and anticipated impact would be helpful. I appreciate the updates to the GitHub repo (installation/usage instructions) and the new dataset overview page; these materially improve reproducibility and clarity. Overall. I will raise my rating.

summary.value:
This paper introduces RGBDT500, a large-scale tri-modal (RGB, Depth, Thermal) tracking dataset with 500 sequences and 203K spatiotemporally aligned frames.
Besides, this work proposes a novel baseline tracker RDTTrack. 
RDTTrack integrates tri-modal data via orthogonal feature projection to reduce depth-thermal redundancy and prompt learning to fuse modalities with a frozen OSTrack backbone. 
Experiments show state-of-the-art performance of the RDTTrack on the proposed RGBDT500 test set.

strengths_contributions.value:
-This work contributes a new dataset for multi-modal tracking.
-This work is clearly organized and accessibly written.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Although some comparative experiments were conducted, I found that the author's experimental section did not conduct any comparative analysis with the currently popular image level fusion tracking method. The author may consider conducting such a comparison to make the article more comprehensive.

- Failure cases demand systematic examination with visual examples and error attribution.

- As a task with high timeliness requirements, the author lacks a detailed analysis and comparison of the running time of different methods for calculating efficiency.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
- The efficiency of the proposed RDTTrack should be analyzed.
- The failure cases of this work should be studied and discussed.
- The authors should propose several concrete possible solutions for the limitations of this work.

final_justification.value: After reading the author's reply and other comments and replies, I think the author has basically solved my doubts, and I decided to keep my rating.

summary.value: The authors introduce RGBDT500, the first tracking dataset that incorporates RGB, depth, and thermal infrared modalities, specifically designed to tackle the challenges associated with tri-modal fusion. Serving as a comprehensive benchmark, RGBDT500 aims to advance research in multi-modal object tracking. Alongside the dataset, they propose RDTTrack, a novel tri-modal tracker that harnesses the complementary strengths of all three input modalities. RDTTrack demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on RGBDT500, thereby validating the effectiveness of tri-modal integration.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper constructs the first video tracking dataset that includes RGB, depth, and thermal infrared modalities, effectively addressing the limitations of RGB-D or RGB-T tracking under challenging conditions such as low illumination, occlusion, and depth blur. The tri-modal setting enhances robustness in complex scenes.

- By incorporating a plug-and-play prompt learning module and orthogonal fusion strategy, the proposed RDTTrack model demonstrates strong adaptability and potential for transfer to other multi-modal tasks beyond RGBDT500.

- The method's effectiveness is thoroughly validated through ablation studies on different modality combinations and key components (e.g., orthogonality constraint, fusion design), forming a solid empirical foundation.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The VTUAV [1] dataset is a UAV-view RGB-T single-object tracking benchmark. However, the paper lacks both qualitative and quantitative comparisons with this dataset.

- The VTUAV dataset also introduces a baseline method, HMFT. A quantitative evaluation of this method on the proposed RGBDT500 dataset should be included for completeness.

[1] Visible-Thermal UAV Tracking: A Large-Scale Benchmark and New Baseline. CVPR 2022.

title.value: Collaborating Vision, Depth, and Thermal Signals for Multi-Modal Tracking: Dataset and Algorithm

TLDR.value: A dataset and an algorithm for multi-modal object tracking.

abstract.value:
Existing multi-modal object tracking approaches primarily focus on dual-modal paradigms, such as RGB-Depth or RGB-Thermal, yet remain challenged in complex scenarios due to limited input modalities. 
To address this gap, this work introduces a novel multi-modal tracking task that leverages three complementary modalities, including visible RGB, Depth (D), and Thermal Infrared (TIR), aiming to enhance robustness in complex scenarios. 
To support this task, we construct a new multi-modal tracking dataset, coined RGBDT500, which consists of 500 videos with synchronised frames across the three modalities. 
Each frame provides spatially aligned RGB, depth, and thermal infrared images with precise object bounding box annotations.
Furthermore, we propose a novel multi-modal tracker, dubbed RDTTrack.
RDTTrack integrates tri-modal information for robust tracking by leveraging a pretrained RGB-only tracking model and prompt learning techniques.
In specific, RDTTrack fuses thermal infrared and depth modalities under a proposed orthogonal projection constraint, then integrates them with RGB signals as prompts for the pre-trained foundation tracking model, effectively harmonising tri-modal complementary cues.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of the proposed method, showing significant improvements over existing dual-modal approaches in terms of tracking accuracy and robustness in complex scenarios. 
The dataset and source code are publicly available at https://xuefeng-zhu5.github.io/RGBDT500.
